passage:
Rohan chose one beginner Python course and pinned a note above his desk: one lesson a day. When friends shared links to other courses, he said, "After mine." Only when the last lesson was done did he write his first little script, a cricket quiz.

Uma, Jaya and Indu met every Friday, each with one solved problem to show. The rule was simple: if someone skipped, the other two messaged them. In dull weeks, those Friday meetings kept all three going.

Dev watched video after video and nodded along. He felt he was learning. Then his teacher opened a blank editor and asked him to write a loop that printed one to ten. His fingers stayed above the keys. All this time he had copied what the screen showed and had never typed a line himself.

Three weeks later, looking over his history, Dev saw nothing new since the start. He deleted the video list from his home screen and started with small exercises. He opened a video only when he was stuck, and typed every line himself.

qa.q: What did Rohan write after finishing the course?
qa.a: He wrote his first little script, a cricket quiz.

qa.q: How did the Friday group's routine differ from Dev's video watching, and what were the results?
qa.a: The group brought one solved problem each week and messaged whoever skipped, which kept all three going, while Dev only followed videos and could not write a loop in a blank editor.

qa.q: What was Dev feeling with his fingers above the keys?
qa.a: Embarrassed and stuck, since he had felt he was learning but could not begin.
Dev could keep solving small exercises first and share his code with a friend at a regular time.

grounding: Four approaches to learning to code online: one course to the end, a study group, hopping between tutorials, and switching method after a review.
